overall: The article's biggest weakness is its omission of planned deliverables and text facts, specifically leaving out the required closing 'SIP myths, checked' table, dropping inflation failure rates from the body of Q1, and misdescribing Figure F.q1's chart type. Its biggest strength is its relentless empirical discipline and clarity, dismantling common industry myths by translating 30 years of market data into intuitive rupee outcomes that vividly demonstrate why staying invested during market drops beats stopping.

answers.q1: Over ten years, an equity SIP never lost money, trailed an FD in only 0.4% of start months, and trailed inflation in 0.8%, though over one to five years it lost money in 7% to 29% of windows and trailed an FD in 16% to 38% (with shorter-horizon inflation failure rates omitted from the text).
answers.q2: An investor should expect a wide range around the median ten-year return of 14.6% a year, with 90% of outcomes falling between 9.8% and 26.0% and extremes ranging from 4.3% to 32.7%.
answers.q3: After inflation, the typical ten-year Nifty 500 SIP earned 8.3% a year (about six percentage points below nominal), with 5% of start months earning under 2.0% and only 0.8% failing to beat inflation outright.
answers.q4: Over ten years, the Midcap 150 delivered the highest median return (17.9%) and Smallcap 250 returned 15.3% but experienced a negative worst case (−0.5%) and a 54% maximum fall, while the Nifty 500 returned 13.5%, gold 8.9%, and government bonds 8.0% with minimal drawdown.
answers.q5: Diversifying into a 60/20/20 mix cost ₹1.4 lakh in median final value over ten years while gaining only ₹0.2 lakh in the 5th-percentile bad case, but over five and fifteen years the bad-case gain exceeded the median cost while roughly halving the worst-case fall from 44% to 25%.
answers.q6: Rebalancing a 60/20/20 SIP annually each April added a median 0.8 percentage points a year over ten years, helping in at least nine in ten start months.
answers.q7: Longer SIPs become dramatically steadier in annualised returns as the 5th-to-95th percentile spread narrows from 41 points at five years to 3.5 points at twenty, but rupee multiples remain wide apart, spanning 4.2 to 6.4 times the invested capital at twenty years.
answers.q8: The start year mattered enormously because ten-year median returns ranged from 9.3% for 2010 starts to 26.5% for 1997 starts, yet starting within 2% of a market peak versus more than 10% below it made almost no difference (13.6% versus 14.9%).
answers.q9: The first five years matter most, contributing 55% of a 15-year SIP's final value compared to 14% from the last five, and de-risking into fixed deposits over the final 36 months proved costly, ending ahead in only 19% of cases and lowering even the 5th-percentile bad case.
answers.q10: To reach ₹1 crore in 15 years on the Nifty 500, an investor needed ₹16,455 a month for a 50% chance, ₹19,459 for an 80% chance, and ₹22,810 for a 95% chance (with a 12% calculator asking for ₹21,011 and succeeding 90% of the time), while starting five years late required ₹21,612 a month over 15 years to match the 20-year outcome.
answers.q11: For an investor holding a lump sum, deploying it immediately beat a 12-month STP in 57% of start months, while for a salaried saver earning monthly, an ongoing monthly SIP beat saving in an FD to invest annually in 73% of start months.
answers.q12: SIP dates, weekly frequency, and valuation-doubling rules barely mattered, shifting ten-year returns by only 0.0 to 0.2 percentage points, whereas pausing during falls cost 2.0 to 3.8 points and a 1% higher expense ratio cost 1.1 points a year.
answers.q13: No, a SIP is not long-term after a year because each instalment has its own one-year clock; after two years, 50% of the units are still short-term (holding 27% of gains) and subject to short-term capital gains tax plus potential exit loads.
answers.q14: Volatility did not reliably help an equity SIP, as the SIP's 0.7 percentage point median return edge over index buy-and-hold correlated only weakly (0.23) with window volatility across the entire history and showed zero correlation after 2005.
answers.q15: Practically all Nifty 500 SIPs went under water at some point (97% of start months), with the deepest fall reaching 44% below invested money and the longest unbroken stretch in the red lasting 38 months.
answers.q16: SIPs in the red at 12 months ended with a higher median ten-year return (17.9% versus 14.1% for the rest) because depressed markets allowed 18% of contributions to purchase 30% of final units, though this bonus did not extend to mid caps or multi-asset mixes.
answers.q17: Stopping a red Nifty 500 SIP never protected the investor, as continuing beat stopping-and-holding, switching to FDs, or pausing in 100% of 12-month red cases, with an FD switch costing a median ₹14.8 lakh.
answers.q18: A SIP's running return does not begin to reliably predict its final outcome until 99 months (over eight years) in, and early returns at 12 months actually correlate negatively (−0.35) with the ten-year ending return.
answers.q19: In the historical record, the bad-start bonus did not depend on cheap valuations, as month-12 red SIPs when P/E was above median finished at 14.3% compared to 14.8% when below median, while currently Nifty 50 P/E stands at the 35th percentile and deposit rates at the 25th percentile.
answers.q20: No, industry SIP money did not arrive at bad times: actual inflows earned 11.2% a year since 2016, trailing a trend-growth benchmark by only 0.1 percentage points.
answers.q21: Market falls of 10% or more have been somewhat shallower and less frequent since 2016 (7 falls with a 16% median depth, down from 11 falls with a 20% median depth), but a single decade is insufficient to prove that SIP inflows caused this moderation.
answers.q22: The implied average life of a SIP account is currently about 1.8 years (never exceeding 4.9 years outside clean-ups), while the stoppage ratio reflects account closures relative to new registrations and spiked to 3.5 during AMFI's 2025 clean-up.
